notes: The whole 36-page adopted PDF, read end to end: the preface and contributors, the theme introduction, the historic context (the Roaring Twenties, the Great Depression, the Modernistic era in San Francisco, Modernistic era architecture), the three sub-themes -- Art Deco 1925-c.1936, Streamline Moderne 1935-1950 and International Style 1935-1965 -- with their narratives, evaluation criteria, eligibility standards, character-defining features and integrity considerations, all 31 figures, and the bibliography. There is no inventory table and no APN anywhere in the document. This statement is an addendum to the Modern Architecture and Landscape Design, 1935-1970 HCS and defers the International Style evaluative framework to it, which is why that sub-theme is two pages where the other two are nine each -- and why the International Style still yields four addresses, all of them figure captions.

coverage.remaining: None. The document was read in full; nothing in it is outstanding.
coverage.note: 25 distinct numbered street addresses across 36 pages; 1487 31st Avenue is illustrated three times and 2501-2515 Ocean Avenue twice, each recorded once. Nearly every address carries an architect or a builder, which is what makes this statement denser per finding than its length suggests: Timothy Pflueger, Andrew H. Knoll, Harold Stoner, John Elkin Dinwiddie, Conrad Kett, G. Albert Lansburgh, Irvine Goldstine, H.C. Baumann, Richard Neutra, Henry Howard and Mario Ciampi, plus the tract builders F. & T. Rossich, L.L. & M.L. Wold, the Golden Gate Investment Company and Claude T. Lindsay. Buildings the statement names with no street number, and so not recorded as findings: the Golden Gate Bridge (Landmark No. 222, Morrow & Morrow, 1936), the Aquatic Park complex, the San Francisco Zoo aviary, George Washington High School, Lawton Elementary School, Stonestown, the Jack Tar hotel, and Richard Neutra's Ford-Aquino duplex, Schiff House and Kahn House where first listed without addresses. Two of the addresses are remodels rather than new construction -- 200-16 Powell Street (1934) and 2205 Mission Street (1937-38) -- and the date recorded is the date of the remodel the statement describes, not of the building.

findings.description: One of five adjacent, nearly identical Streamline Moderne houses built in 1938 by the Golden Gate Investment Company. This one has been heavily altered — a new window opening and sash, a new garage door, brick cladding at the ground storey and the glass block accents removed — leaving only the speed lines and chimney stack of the original design. It would have qualified as significant as built, but its compromised integrity renders it ineligible; of the five, just one retains its integrity.

findings.description: A Streamline Moderne multi-family residence of 1946 in the Mission — a district with few of them. Postwar, but still a good example of the style: a flat roof with coping, stucco cladding, rounded corners and curved surfaces, curved railings, porthole windows, continuous windows at the building corners, a vestibule entrance and glass blocks. Eligible as a district contributor, though it would need a more exuberant display to qualify individually.
